title: Geothermal reservoirs engineered economically in ordinary deep rock

concept.text: The innovation would make it routine to create a productive geothermal reservoir in hot rock that lacks adequate natural fluid pathways. Engineers would establish connected flow paths between wells, circulate fluid through the heated rock and recover useful heat at the surface. The target is a reservoir that remains productive and economical for years across varied geological settings. Creating fractures and demonstrating short-term heat extraction are necessary steps, but do not establish that broader capability.

Scope synthesis: “ordinary deep rock” means extending deployment beyond unusually favorable naturally permeable geothermal reservoirs. It does not mean that every rock formation, depth or location would be suitable. The central advance concerns subsurface reservoir engineering, drawing on drilling, geomechanics, hydrology, geochemistry and energy engineering. Heat could be used directly; electricity would additionally require suitable temperatures and conversion technology.

significance.text: The potentially revolutionary change is expanded access to geothermal resources. If engineers could reliably create durable, productive fluid pathways, useful geothermal heat could become available in places where hot rock exists but natural permeability is inadequate. This is a conditional inference from the reservoir-creation mechanism documented at FORGE, not a demonstrated finding that widespread hot rock can already be developed economically.

Conditional impact synthesis: successful replication could broaden the locations able to supply geothermal heat and, where temperatures and conversion performance permit, electricity. The impact would depend on the complete project: drilling and well construction, sustained reservoir output, power conversion, finance, transmission or access to heat users, water management and local geology. Reservoir engineering alone would not establish commercially viable energy supply everywhere, and the supplied evidence supports no numerical estimate of global deployment or energy contribution.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is repeatable creation of reservoirs that sustain useful heat extraction for years at acceptable total cost. Connected fractures must support circulation with sufficiently stable pressure and production, adequate water recovery and manageable thermal decline. Short tests cannot resolve whether these properties persist as operation continues. The supplied DOE account identifies sustained circulation, reservoir longevity, water loss, heat extraction and operating measurements relevant to economics as reasons for extended testing.

Broader engineering synthesis: the challenge involves the interacting behavior of heat, flowing fluids and deforming heterogeneous rock. A complete assessment should also examine chemical alteration and induced seismicity alongside water loss and thermal decline. These remain scientifically material concerns in the proposed capability, but the supplied article does not substantiate their mechanisms, severity or management at FORGE. Its omission of them neither resolves those concerns nor demonstrates that they are absent.

Transferability synthesis: a successful reservoir design must be adaptable to contrasting rock conditions without depending on exceptional natural permeability. Establishing that adaptability requires more than repeating a circulation test at one site. The unresolved engineering question is whether reservoir creation, sustained operation and their costs can remain acceptable as geological conditions change.

current_state.text: DOE’s August 17, 2026 account reports that engineered geothermal flow paths and short-term heat extraction had already been demonstrated at Utah FORGE. It describes well stimulation and fracture-network creation in April 2024, followed by a 30-day circulation test in August 2024. These are concrete achievements in reservoir creation and circulation at that research site; they do not establish years of economical production or applicability across contrasting geology.

The same article reports the commencement of an extended circulation test in August 2026, with months of operation intended. Its purpose was to investigate reservoir stability, pressure and production behavior, water recovery, heat extraction and implications for project economics. At the announcement date, these were objectives for longer-duration assessment. The test’s commencement should not be represented as a completed demonstration of long-term commercial performance.

Evidence boundary: the supplied review describes the retained DOE article as complete, identity-verified and untruncated, with no extraction issues recorded in the source index. There is therefore no identified partial-access limitation for this source. However, the review’s bounded freshness-search record is empty, so it cannot establish developments after the August announcement through November 1, 2026, or a comprehensive later state of the field. The supplied material provides no numerical long-term cost, heat-output, water-recovery or thermal-decline results. These limits leave subsequent performance unresolved; they do not invalidate the dated achievements.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independently documented projects in several contrasting geological settings should sustain commercially meaningful heat production for years. Replication should include formations without unusually favorable natural permeability. This would test both durability and transferability. The proposal extends the DOE article’s stated rationale for sustained circulation to assess reservoir longevity and economics; it is not an established DOE requirement.
completion_criteria.label: Sustained commercially meaningful heat for years across contrasting geological settings

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reporting requirements: each project should disclose delivered heat, operating duration, pressure and production stability, water injected and recovered, thermal decline and full-cycle costs, including drilling, reservoir creation and ongoing operation. Chemical changes and induced seismicity should also be documented. Independent assessment should have enough operational and geological information to evaluate performance and whether favorable site selection explains the result.
completion_criteria.label: Disclosed reservoir performance and full-cycle costs enable independent assessment

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: define commercially meaningful output, acceptable cost, water losses, thermal decline and seismic performance explicitly for each intended application before judging success. Heat supply and electricity generation require different performance assessments. No numerical pass thresholds are established by the supplied evidence. Successful finite demonstrations would establish breadth within the tested geological and operating conditions, rather than literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Application-specific performance criteria are predefined, with demonstrated limits stated

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: GEO-01, “Reliable short-term forecasting of damaging earthquakes,” overlaps through fault behavior, rock deformation and the proposed need to assess induced seismicity. GEO-03 would require understanding and managing seismic effects associated with reservoir operations; it would not itself establish reliable short-term forecasting of damaging earthquakes. GEO-10, “Reliable transferable forecasting of volcanic eruptions,” likewise shares questions about subsurface fluids, heat and changing rock conditions, but concerns forecasting volcanic behavior rather than constructing a heat-producing reservoir.

Roster-based synthesis: GEO-02, “A chemically and thermally resolved map of Earth’s deep interior,” overlaps in understanding subsurface temperature, composition and structure. GEO-03 requires site-scale knowledge sufficient to engineer and operate reservoirs, rather than a comprehensive deep-interior map. GEO-08, “Establishing when and how sustained plate tectonics began,” concerns the history of Earth’s thermal and mechanical evolution; geothermal reservoir success would not resolve the timing or origin of sustained plate tectonics.

Roster-based synthesis: GEO-04, “Global-scale, verifiable mineral storage of carbon dioxide,” shares subsurface fluid transport, rock–fluid interaction and verification of performance over time. Its objective is durable carbon storage, whereas GEO-03 seeks sustained heat extraction. GEO-06, “Discovery of globally consequential recoverable geological hydrogen,” shares questions of geological resource access, wells, fluid behavior and recoverability, but targets a recoverable chemical fuel rather than heat from an engineered reservoir.

Roster-based synthesis: GEO-05, “Recovery of a detailed geological record of Earth’s first half-billion years,” and GEO-07, “Reconstructing the Moon-forming impact from independent geological evidence,” are primarily historical reconstruction problems. Their connection to GEO-03 is through geological characterization and interpretation, not a shared completion criterion. GEO-09, “Predictive laws linking erosion, sediment transport and landscape evolution,” shares the ambition of transferable prediction across heterogeneous geological settings, but addresses surface landscape processes rather than engineered deep-rock circulation.

change_log.change: Clarified the concept as durable, economical reservoir creation across varied hot-rock settings, while preserving GEO-03 and its original title.
change_log.reason: Existing engineered flow paths do not establish the broader proposed capability, and “ordinary deep rock” should not imply universal geological suitability.

change_log.change: Separated source-documented operating challenges from the broader concerns of chemical alteration, induced seismicity and coupled rock–fluid–heat behavior.
change_log.reason: The review found support for longevity, water loss, thermal decline and operating stability, but the supplied article does not establish the complete original problem statement.

change_log.change: Preserved the August 2024 30-day test and added the April 2024 reservoir-creation chronology reported in the review.
change_log.reason: These details distinguish demonstrated reservoir creation and short-term circulation from the missing long-term capability.

change_log.change: Described the August 2026 extended test as commenced, with months of operation intended, and retained its specific assessment objectives.
change_log.reason: An announced test and its objectives cannot be treated as completed evidence of durable commercial performance.

change_log.change: Integrated conditional significance with limits on geological suitability, electricity conversion and supporting project infrastructure.
change_log.reason: Expanded geothermal access is a coherent potential consequence, while widespread economical deployment remains unproven.

change_log.change: Expanded completion criteria into proposed demonstrations, reporting requirements and application-specific performance boundaries.
change_log.reason: The review supported broader replication as a useful proposal while identifying the need for explicit commercial thresholds and limits on generality.

change_log.change: Preserved source completeness and the missing freshness-search record as separate evidence limitations.
change_log.reason: The retained article has no reported extraction problem, but its completeness cannot establish subsequent developments or comprehensive field coverage.

change_log.change: Explained relationships to every other supplied roster entry using explicitly labeled synthesis.
change_log.reason: The concepts have relevant overlaps without sharing the same scientific objective or completion criteria.

unresolved_issues: Results and subsequent developments from the extended circulation program after the August 17, 2026 announcement are not established by the supplied evidence.
The supplied source does not establish the mechanisms, magnitude or management of chemical alteration and induced seismicity at FORGE, or substantiate the full coupled-behavior description.
Years-long heat production, full-cycle economics and transferable performance across contrasting geological settings remain unestablished in this record.
Commercially meaningful heat output and acceptable cost, water loss, thermal decline and seismic performance require explicit application-specific thresholds; none are supplied.
The number and range of geological settings needed to demonstrate convincing transferability remain a proposed evaluation-design question.

brief.title: Affordable heat from deep rock in more places
possible: More communities and businesses could draw useful heat from deep underground, even where hot rock lacks natural paths for water to flow. Engineers would connect wells through cracks in the rock and circulate water to bring the heat to the surface.
why: Reliable, affordable reservoirs would widen access to geothermal energy, meaning heat from inside the Earth. More places could supply heat directly to users or generate electricity where the rock is hot enough.

sources.showed: The team created connected cracks between wells and extracted heat during a month-long circulation test. It subsequently began a longer test to study sustained operation.
sources.quote: the team successfully stimulated the production and injection wells, creating the fracture network that forms the reservoir.
sources.cited_for: Engineers have created underground flow paths and used them to recover heat.
sources.not_established: These tests do not establish economical production lasting years across different kinds of rock.

sources.showed: A flow test at Fenton Hill ran in segments over 14 months. The produced water showed no discernible temperature decline.
sources.quote: with no discernable temperature decline of the produced fluid.
sources.cited_for: Heat extraction has continued beyond short tests without an observed fall in water temperature.
sources.not_established: The test did not demonstrate years of commercially viable operation or repeatability across contrasting geological settings.

sources.who: Pengju Xing, Kevin England, Joseph Moore and John McLennan
sources.showed: At Utah FORGE, forcing water and sand into the rock improved flow through cracks. Water recovery reached 90% by the end of the longer circulation test.
sources.quote:
demonstrated a significant improvement in reservoir conductivity and fluid recovery 
following commercial-scale hydraulic stimulation.
sources.cited_for: Creating and supporting cracks improved water flow and recovery between wells.
sources.not_established: Improved circulation over a short test does not establish lasting heat output or acceptable total costs.

shown: Fenton Hill has demonstrated longer heat extraction, while Utah FORGE has demonstrated improved circulation and water recovery. FORGE also began an extended test to investigate durability. Neither project has established the full combination of lasting output, affordable operation and success across contrasting rock conditions.
missing: Reservoirs must deliver useful heat for years at an acceptable total cost, including drilling, reservoir creation and operation.
Water recovery, pressure and heat output must remain adequate as the rock cools during continued operation.
Successful reservoir designs must work across contrasting rock conditions without relying on unusually favorable natural flow paths.

milestones.label: Useful heat lasts for years across different rock settings
milestones.explanation: Independently documented projects would have to sustain commercially useful heat for years across contrasting settings, including rock with poor natural water flow. This would establish durability and adaptability.

milestones.label: Performance and total costs allow independent assessment
milestones.explanation: Projects would have to disclose heat output, operating duration, pressure, flow, water recovery, cooling, chemical changes, triggered earthquakes and total costs. Independent assessment could then judge performance and site advantages.

milestones.label: Success criteria and demonstrated limits are explicit
milestones.explanation: Each application would need predefined criteria for useful output, cost, water loss, cooling and earthquake effects, with demonstrated limits stated. This would clarify what success means for heat supply or electricity.

uncertain: How much chemical change and how many earthquakes might operation trigger, and how effectively could these effects be managed?
What output, cost, water loss and cooling would be acceptable for each intended use?
How many contrasting rock settings would establish that reservoir designs can transfer reliably?

page.title: Enhanced geothermal electricity at $45/MWh
page.definition: Enhanced geothermal systems (EGS) circulate fluid through engineered fractures in hot rock that lacks sufficient natural permeability, or connected paths for fluid flow. The capability is electricity generation at a levelized, or lifetime-average, cost of at most US$45/MWh in the DOE target’s 2019-dollar accounting.

goal.need: In its 2024 assessment, the IEA reported that geothermal met less than 1% of global energy demand, while geothermal generating capacity averaged over 75% utilisation in 2023. Conventional geothermal generation requires heat, fluid and connected rock pathways. EGS creates pathways where natural permeability is insufficient, extending access beyond naturally productive reservoirs.

statements.quote: Geothermal can provide around-the-clock electricity generation, heat production and storage.
make enhanced geothermal systems (EGS) a widespread renewable energy option in the U.S.
statements.context: The stated purpose of the Enhanced Geothermal Shot announced on 8 September 2022.

statements.body: U.S. Department of Energy, EGS Pilot Demonstrations programme
statements.quote: demonstrate EGS in a variety of geographic locations, geologic formations, and subsurface conditions.

completion.title: EGS electricity reaches an unsubsidized levelized cost of at most US$45/MWh.
completion.criterion: EGS electricity reaches an unsubsidized levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) of no more than US$45/MWh, using the 2019-dollar basis of the analysis underpinning DOE’s Enhanced Geothermal Shot. Assessment includes exploration, drilling, reservoir development, well flow and power-plant operation. DOE identifies model-based LCOE values as its primary metric; it specifies no mandatory field-test duration or site-count qualification for this cost target.
completion.set_by: U.S. Department of Energy, Enhanced Geothermal Shot announcement; accounting explained in NREL’s supporting analysis and DOE’s 2025 assessment report.
completion.threshold_quote: cutting its cost by 90% to $45 per megawatt hour
completion.basis: The Shot supplies a published numerical meaning for economical EGS electricity. Its supporting analysis includes reservoir construction and power production, making the target relevant to the complete system. DOE’s assessment uses model-based costs. Meeting this economic target alone would not establish a specified number of operating years or successful replication across every geological setting.

milestones.title: An engineered geothermal reservoir circulates fluid between wells and returns rock heat to the surface.
milestones.criterion: Injected fluid circulates through an engineered fracture network between injection and production wells and returns recovered rock heat to the surface. Utah FORGE tested one well pair for 26.8 days, from 8 August 2024 to 4 September 2024; final production was 26.5 kg/s at 196°C, with a corrected production-to-injection ratio of 90%. DOE announced an extended circulation test on 17 August 2026; that announcement reported commencement rather than completed long-duration performance.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Department of Energy, EGS development sequence, Step 2: Create a Reservoir.
milestones.threshold_quote: The resulting circulation loop allows water to flow through the enhanced reservoir, picking up in situ heat.

milestones.title: An engineered geothermal reservoir supports 5 MW of electricity generation.
milestones.criterion: Create an EGS reservoir capable of supporting 5 MW of electricity generation, DOE’s published technical demonstration target. On 1 October 2026, Fervo reported that the first Cape Station GeoBlock had produced 33 MW net and reached contractual commercial operation. This company announcement is not peer reviewed and does not establish lifetime reservoir performance.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Department of Energy Geothermal Technologies Office, EGS programme strategy reported in its 2013 technology roadmap.
milestones.threshold_quote: demonstrate the ability to create a 5MW reservoir

milestones.title: An EGS reservoir sustains 80 kg/s at a wellhead temperature of 250 ± 10°C for six years.
milestones.criterion: Operate an EGS reservoir for six years at 80 kg/s with a wellhead temperature of 250 ± 10°C. This is a historical DOE research benchmark, not a universal minimum temperature for economical EGS. At Fenton Hill, one Phase-2 reservoir underwent segmented flow testing over 14 months during 1992 and 1993, with no discernible produced-fluid temperature decline. That observation does not establish the six-year flow-and-temperature benchmark.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Department of Energy Geothermal Technologies Program, published 2008 draft multi-year plan, section 4.2.1.1, printed page 85.
milestones.threshold_quote: an EGS reservoir able to operate for six years at 80 kg/s with wellhead temperature of 250+/- 10°C

milestones.title: Next-generation geothermal demonstrations cover 5–10 separate geologic settings.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrations cover 5–10 separate geologic settings, DOE’s published validation-suite benchmark. The benchmark was written for next-generation geothermal collectively, including EGS and closed-loop systems. DOE’s EGS pilot selections include Utah, volcanic Oregon and Pennsylvania’s Utica Shale; selection and project objectives do not establish completed operation across those settings.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Department of Energy, 2024 Commercial Liftoff report, Chapter 3; the published benchmark covers next-generation geothermal collectively.

milestones.title: EGS electricity reaches DOE’s US$60–70/MWh national-average liftoff cost range.
milestones.criterion: Reach DOE’s interim national-average EGS LCOE range of US$60–70/MWh without subsidies. The Liftoff report associates this range with overnight capital cost of US$4,700–5,000/kW and explicitly places it before the $45/MWh Shot target. Its approximately US$14,700/kW estimate for first-of-a-kind EGS in 2023 is a cost estimate, not evidence that the interim LCOE range has been attained.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Department of Energy, 2024 Commercial Liftoff report, Chapters 2 and 3.

not_found: No published regulator or standards-body qualification combining the cost target, a fixed operating duration and a geology replication count was found.
No completed six-year reservoir test meeting the quoted 80 kg/s and 250 ± 10°C conditions was found.
No dated final performance report for the FORGE extended circulation test announced on 17 August 2026 was found.
No operating-data-based assessment establishing the national-average liftoff cost range or the Shot cost target was found.
No formal rule for counting separate geologic settings was found in DOE’s Liftoff report.
